claims.text: FeNiCrMn is obtained by removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Removing Co lowers the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Changes in stacking-fault energy modulate competition between dislocation motion and planar-defect formation.
The competition between dislocation glide and transient stacking-fault formation in FeNiCrMn is highly sensitive to both temperature and strain rate.
Low temperature and high strain rate increase dislocation entanglement and transient stacking-fault formation in FeNiCrMn.
The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
In situ advanced TEM or synchrotron experiments can be used to track deformation-induced microstructural evolution.
The proposed tests span approximately 77–500 K and quasi-static through high-rate loading.
Dislocation networks and transient stacking faults are the structural mediators of the proposed dynamic behavior.
Dislocation entanglements and planar defects impede further dislocation motion and thereby enhance strength or strain hardening.
The same defect structures provide channels for plastic accommodation and thus help preserve ductility.
Under low-temperature, high-rate loading, FeNiCrMn will have a higher transient stacking-fault density than CoCrFeMnNi.
Under low-temperature, high-rate loading, FeNiCrMn will show more pronounced dislocation entanglement than CoCrFeMnNi.
The additional transient stacking faults and dislocation entanglements will give FeNiCrMn a better strength–ductility balance than CoCrFeMnNi.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is the controlled baseline alloy.
The proposed mechanism dominates from approximately 77 K to 500 K and from quasi-static to high-rate loading.
Minor composition differences and characterization resolution can affect inferred defect densities and spatial distributions.
Deformation nanotwinning may concurrently modify the observed behavior.
Dislocation density, transient stacking-fault density, and stress–strain response will be measured in both alloys as functions of temperature and strain rate.

Failure of FeNiCrMn to show significantly higher transient stacking-fault density and altered dislocation networks under low-temperature, high-rate conditions would falsify the proposed mediation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The core mechanism is specifically associated with low temperature and high strain rate, whereas the boundary says it dominates across the entire 77–500 K range and from quasi-static through high-rate loading. This overextends the stated regime without explaining behavior at the warmer or slower limits.
